goals: Use the dative forms of articles, possessives and personal pronouns
Use verbs with the dative and put two objects in the right order
Choose the right case after prepositions, including Wo? and Wohin?
Give adjectives the right ending before a noun
Compare things with the comparative and the superlative

title.t: dem Mann, der Frau, den Kindern – mir, dir, ihm
title.s: The dative: articles, possessives and pronouns

grammar.explain:
The **dative** is the case for the **person who receives** something or who an action is for. English often shows this with *to* or *for*: *I'm giving the key **to my sister***. → Ich gebe **meiner Schwester** den Schlüssel. The question word is **wem?** (*to whom?*). Some verbs and prepositions also take the dative – you'll practice them in the next lessons.
The articles change like this: der → **dem**, das → **dem**, die → **der**, plural die → **den**. **ein, kein** and the possessives **mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr** take the same endings: **einem** Freund, **einer** Freundin, **meinem** Kind, **unseren** Gästen.
In the **dative plural** the noun itself also gets **-n**: die Kinder → **den Kindern**, die Freunde → **den Freunden**. There is no extra -n when the plural already ends in **-n** or **-s**: **den Eltern, den Frauen, den Autos**.
The personal pronouns: ich → **mir**, du → **dir**, er → **ihm**, sie → **ihr**, es → **ihm**, wir → **uns**, ihr → **euch**, sie → **ihnen**, Sie → **Ihnen**.
Careful: English uses *to* and Persian uses *be* for the receiver (*ketab ra be u dadam* – *I gave the book to him*), but German shows it with the case alone: Ich gebe **ihm** das Buch – not *zu ihm*. Also watch the forms that look alike: **der** is also the dative of **die** (Ich helfe **der** Frau), and **ihr** can mean *you all*, *to her* or, as a possessive, *her* and *their*.

title.t: Ich helfe dir. Ich gebe dir den Schlüssel.
title.s: Verbs with the dative; dative and accusative objects

grammar.explain:
Some German verbs always take a **dative object**, even though English uses a normal object. The most important ones are **helfen** (*to help*), **danken** (*to thank*), **gefallen** (*to please, to appeal to*), **gehören** (*to belong to*), **schmecken** (*to taste good*) and **passen** (*to fit, to suit*): **Ich helfe dir.** **Wir danken Ihnen.**
With **gefallen, schmecken, gehören** and **passen**, the thing is the **subject** and the person is in the **dative**, so the verb agrees with the thing: **Der Rock gefällt mir.** **Die Schuhe gefallen mir.** **Schmeckt dir die Suppe?** Use **schmecken** for food and drink, **gefallen** for things you see, wear or experience.
Verbs of giving and showing – **geben, schenken, zeigen, bringen, schicken, kaufen** – often have two objects: the **person** in the **dative** and the **thing** in the **accusative**: Ich schenke **meiner Tante eine Kerze**.
Word order: with two nouns, the dative comes first: Ich gebe **dem Kind den Ball**. A pronoun comes before a noun: Ich gebe **ihm den Ball**. Ich gebe **ihn dem Kind**. With two pronouns, the accusative comes first: Ich gebe **ihn ihm**.
Careful: *I help you* is **Ich helfe dir**, not *dich* – Persian speakers have it easier here, because Persian also helps *to* someone: *be kasi komak kardan*. And *I like the skirt* is not *Ich gefalle den Rock* but **Der Rock gefällt mir**: the skirt is the subject.
table: Ich gebe dem Kind den Ball.

title.t: mit dem Bus, zur Arbeit – für dich, ohne mich
title.s: Prepositions with the dative or the accusative

grammar.explain:
Many prepositions always take the same case, whatever the verb is. Learn them in two groups.
With the **dative**: **aus** (*from, out of*), **bei** (*at someone's place, at a company*), **mit** (*with, by*), **nach** (*after; to* a city or country), **seit** (*since, for*), **von** (*from, of*), **zu** (*to*): **aus der Küche, bei meiner Tante, mit dem Bus, nach dem Essen, seit einer Woche, von meinem Chef, zu meinen Freunden**. Short forms are normal: **zu dem → zum, zu der → zur, bei dem → beim, von dem → vom**.
With the **accusative**: **für** (*for*), **ohne** (*without*), **gegen** (*against*; with times *around, about*), **um** (*around*; with clock times *at*), **durch** (*through*): **für meinen Sohn, ohne dich, gegen den Wind, um die Ecke, durch die Stadt**. In the accusative only the masculine looks different: **den, einen, meinen**.
**seit** goes with the **present tense** for something that is still going on: **Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch.** – *I have been learning German for a year.*
Careful: English *to* can be **zu, nach** or **in**, and *from* can be **aus** or **von**: **aus** is for origin and *out of* (**aus dem Iran, aus dem Haus**), **von** for a starting point or a person (**von der Arbeit, von Sara**). Don't use the dative after **für** or **ohne**: **für dich**, not *für dir*. And *by train* is **mit dem Zug** – not *mit Zug*.

title.t: Wo? in der Küche – Wohin? in die Küche

grammar.explain:
Nine prepositions can take either the **dative** or the **accusative**: **in, an, auf, unter, über, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen**. The case depends on the question.
**Wo?** (*where?*) – something is in a place and doesn't move to a new place → **dative**: Die Tasche liegt **auf dem** Stuhl. **Wohin?** (*where to?*) – something moves to a new place → **accusative**: Ich lege die Tasche **auf den** Stuhl.
The verb usually tells you the question. **stellen, legen, hängen, gehen, fahren, bringen** answer **wohin?**; **stehen, liegen, hängen, sitzen, sein, wohnen, arbeiten** answer **wo?**. Upright things **stehen** (you **stellen** them there), flat things **liegen** (you **legen** them there), and **hängen** is used for both: Ich hänge das Bild **an die** Wand. Das Bild hängt **an der** Wand.
Short forms: **in dem → im, an dem → am, in das → ins, an das → ans**: im Bad, ins Bad, am Fenster, ans Fenster.
Careful: English and Persian often use the same word in both sentences (*on the table*), so ask yourself every time: does something move to a new place? Movement inside one place is still **wo?**: Die Kinder laufen **im** Park. And don't mix up **stellen** (*to put*) and **stehen** (*to stand*): Ich **stelle** die Flasche auf den Tisch. Die Flasche **steht** auf dem Tisch.

title.t: der neue Tisch, ein neuer Tisch
title.s: Adjective endings after der and after ein

grammar.explain:
After **sein**, an adjective has no ending: **Der Tisch ist neu.** But **before a noun**, an adjective always has an ending: **der neue Tisch, ein neuer Tisch**. The ending depends on the article, the gender, the case and the number.
After **der, die, das** (and **dieser, welcher, jeder**) there are only two endings: **-e** in the nominative singular (**der alte Mann, die alte Frau, das alte Haus**) and in the feminine and neuter accusative (**die alte Frau, das alte Haus**). **-en** everywhere else: the masculine accusative (**den alten Mann**), the whole dative (**dem alten Mann, der alten Frau**) and all plurals (**die alten Häuser**).
After **ein, kein** and **mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr**, the endings are the same with three exceptions – the forms where the article itself has no ending. There the adjective shows the gender: masculine nominative **-er** (**ein alter Mann**, -er as in **der**), neuter nominative and accusative **-es** (**ein altes Haus**, -es as in **das**). In the plural, **keine, meine** and the other possessives are followed by **-en**: **meine alten Freunde**.
Careful: in English the adjective never changes, and in Persian it comes after the noun, joined to it by the ezafe *-e*, and doesn't change either (*ketab-e bozorg*). In German it comes before the noun and needs an ending. Don't forget the **-en** in the dative: **mit dem neuen Auto, in einer kleinen Wohnung**. And **teuer** loses an e before an ending: **ein teures Kleid**.

title.t: größer als, so groß wie, am größten

grammar.explain:
To compare two people or things, add **-er** to the adjective and use **als** (*than*): **Der Zug ist schneller als der Bus.** This works for long adjectives too – German has no word like *more* here: **interessant → interessanter** (*more interesting*).
The **superlative** is **am** + adjective + **-sten**: **am schnellsten, am billigsten**. After **-d, -t, -s, -ß, -z** it's **-esten**: **am ältesten, am kürzesten** – but **am größten**. Before a noun, comparatives and superlatives take the normal adjective endings: **mein älterer Bruder, das schnellste Auto**.
Many short adjectives get an **umlaut**: **alt – älter, jung – jünger, groß – größer, kurz – kürzer, lang – länger, warm – wärmer, kalt – kälter**. **teuer** loses an e: **teurer**. The most important irregular forms are **gut – besser – am besten, viel – mehr – am meisten, gern – lieber – am liebsten**. With a verb, **gern, lieber, am liebsten** mean *like (doing), prefer (doing), like (doing) best*: Ich trinke gern Tee, aber **lieber** Kaffee.
For two equal things use **so … wie** (*as … as*): **Lena ist so groß wie ich.** **nicht so … wie** means *not as … as*.
Careful: after a comparative always use **als** – not **wie**, and not **von**, even though Persian uses *az* (*from*) for *than*. English speakers: don't say *mehr schnell*, and remember that *than* is **als**, not **dann**. **mehr** never takes an ending: **mehr Zeit, mehr Freunde**.
